entries.title: Path-Independent Deleveraging Rules
entries.summary: We characterise path-independent auto-deleveraging (ADL) rules as an extended log-exponential family. Immunity to account splitting, merging and reopening further restrict the class. Homogeneity (essentially) restricts the class to a one-parameter family ordered by both fairness and platform risk. Its split-proof members continuously interpolate between proportional division and water-filling. Among these rules, decreasing the parameter reduces risk at the cost of increasing inequality in how accounts are treated. This suggests selecting the parameter through an ex-ante calibration to a risk bound on historical data to choose a maximally fair rule subject to that bound. A counterfactual replay of Hyperliquid's ADL episode on 10 October 2025 finds that a range of intermediate parameters significantly improves on the observed allocation in both burden dispersion and subsequent risk statistics.

entries.title: The Rate of Convergence of Empirical $(p,q)$-Gromov-Wasserstein Distances
entries.summary: We study empirical convergence rates for $(p,q)$-Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distances $D_{p,q}$ for arbitrary real exponents $p>0$ and $q\ge1$. Let $μ$ and $ν$ be probability measures on compact metric spaces $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$, and let $\widehatμ_n$ and $\widehatν_m$ be their empirical measures, constructed from independent i.i.d. samples of sizes $n$ and $m$. If the spaces $\mathcal{X},\,\mathcal{Y}$ are compact subsets of the Euclidean spaces $\mathbb{R}^{d_x}$ and $\mathbb{R}^{d_y}$, respectively, we obtain an upper bound of order $(n\wedge m)^{-(p\wedge2)/((d_x\wedge d_y)\vee 2(p\wedge2))}$ on the plug-in error of $D_{p,q}^p(\widehatμ_n,\widehatν_m)$ in expectation, up to a logarithmic factor at the critical dimension $d_x\wedge d_y=2(p\wedge2)$. On Euclidean balls, this rate is sharp up to the logarithmic factor. More generally, we show that the same upper bound holds when one space is a compact subset of a complete, connected $d$-dimensional Riemannian manifold and the other has polynomial covering numbers, with $d_x\wedge d_y$ replaced by $d$. Earlier works on $(2,2)$-GW, $(2,1)$-GW and other even-order cases rely on variational representations of GW distances that are specific to their exponents. We instead reduce the plug-in error to an analysis of empirical processes through local duality, which may be of independent interest.

entries.title: Flow Matching from Non-Gaussian Sources: A Theory of Efficient Sampling
entries.summary: Flow matching is a versatile framework for generative modeling that transports a source distribution to a target data distribution. A key advantage is its flexibility in the choice of source distribution, such as heavy-tailed and multimodal sources. Yet finite-step sampling guarantees for non-Gaussian sources remain limited. We establish a nonasymptotic convergence theory for Euler discretization of flow matching with linear interpolation. Suppose the source distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ has an everywhere positive, continuously differentiable density, finite total variance $\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}$, and an $L$-Lipschitz score. Using the population velocity field and a suitable time grid, this sampler achieves total variation error at most $\varepsilon$ in $\widetilde{O}(Ld\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}/\varepsilon)$ iterations, provided the target distribution satisfies a mild second-moment condition. These assumptions cover, among many examples, source distributions such as multivariate Student's $t$ distributions with more than two degrees of freedom and finite Gaussian mixtures with shared covariance, while accommodating target distributions with neither a smooth density nor bounded support.

entries.title: Learning from Context: Leave-One-Out Prediction in Jump Diffusions
entries.summary: Continuous diffusion models generate discrete data through stochastic dynamics in an embedding space. We consider jump diffusions that additionally reset coordinates to embeddings of categorical values. A coordinate's own corrupted state can make prediction easy, potentially reducing the pressure to learn dependencies between coordinates. We study leave-one-out (LOO) prediction, in which each coordinate is predicted from the corrupted states of the other coordinates. We show that, under stated assumptions, jump diffusions with complete coordinate resets and state-independent clocks preserve the prescribed marginals when reset destinations use exact LOO probabilities and the drift uses the full endpoint posterior. We further show that this drift can be constructed from LOO probabilities by analytic likelihood completion without additional network evaluations. We evaluate unrestricted, LOO, and completed predictions on Text8 and LM1B text generation and ZINC250k molecular graph generation. LOO-based variants improve key generation metrics over matched unrestricted controls on all three datasets. Controlled interventions assess reliance on local inputs and context, and we analyze the effect of analytic likelihood completion.

entries.title: Mamba Flow Matching Neural Processes: Linear-Time Inference for Irregularly Observed Spatial Fields
entries.summary: Interpolating a spatial field, such as daily maximum temperature, from sparse, irregularly located observations recurs across the environmental and health sciences. Standard Gaussian-process kriging refits hyperparameters and solves an $O(N^3)$ system for every new field. When many related fields are observed, such as daily maps from one sensor network, neural processes (NPs) instead learn the interpolation map from past fields and predict a new field in one forward pass. Joint-predictive variants, which sample whole fields rather than independent per-location values, typically use self-attention over context and query points, costing $O(K^2)$ in the combined point count $K$ and limiting practical use to a few thousand points. State-space models offer a linear-time alternative, but a direct state-space adaptation compresses the context into one hidden state before reading queries, reducing what the decoder sees. We propose MambaFlowNP, a linear-compute joint-predictive NP trained with conditional flow matching. A multi-directional Mamba-2 scan reads context and query tokens in one shared sequence, so each query's velocity is read from its own scan position rather than a compressed context summary, and because queries only read the scan state, predictions are consistent across query sets. MambaFlowNP is competitive with the strongest attention-based joint-predictive baselines on synthetic Matérn Gaussian-process benchmarks, and on regional to continental-scale NOAA temperature interpolation it attains the lowest RMSE and CRPS and near-nominal coverage on every tier, while running 114--784$\times$ faster than the strongest joint-predictive baseline. A single forward pass scales to $10^6$ points on one NVIDIA L40S GPU in under a second. This makes joint prediction feasible for continental-scale, irregularly sampled sensor networks; predictive quality is evaluated up to $K=5{,}580$.

entries.title: A Three-Factor Hull-White Scenario Generator for Macro-Financial Stress Forecasting
entries.summary: This paper builds a scenario engine that maps a yield-curve path into a distribution of macro-financial outcomes. A three-factor Hull-White model generates arbitrage-free curves whose factors are simulated under the physical measure, with an estimated and reported market price of risk. A Minnesota-prior VARX maps the simulated curves into weekly equity returns, the federal funds rate, the Weekly Economic Index, inflation and a bank Marginal Expected Shortfall proxy, with a sign-restricted policy shock adapted to weekly data. Evaluated out of sample from 2017 to 2024, the term-structure block has the lowest forecast error in 13 of 20 maturity and horizon cells, and the density forecasts are well calibrated for the continuously moving variables. At weekly frequency the curve carries no incremental information about these variables once their own lags are controlled for, so the engine's value lies in conditioning on a specified curve path, which no benchmark can do.

entries.title: Reward misalignment as an opportunity for materials discovery
entries.summary: Reward misalignment is usually regarded as a failure of artificial intelligence. In materials discovery with generative AI models, however, disagreement between predefined rewards and expert judgment may reveal materials that the rewards overlook. We investigate this possibility using electronic flat bands as a prime example. Experts mostly agree with a numerical bandwidth score, but their disagreements are systematic and cannot be explained by an estimated 5% rate of mistaken labels. We learn the experts' preferences from pairwise comparisons and use them to guide a crystal diffusion model. The learned preferences and numerical score agree on the flattest bands but diverge elsewhere. For example, the preferences favor KCo2As2 and CoGa, reported compounds with partially flat bands that the score would discard. The framework also extends to synthesizability and phonon properties. Our findings suggest that reward misalignment can expose opportunities for materials discovery beyond what fixed rewards are designed to find.
entries.comment: 33 pages (15 pages main text and 18 pages Supplementary Information), 4 figures

entries.title: Feasible sub-replicating portfolios for basket options via the block rearrangement algorithm
entries.summary: We construct sub-replicating portfolios of vanilla options for a basket call when the marginal distributions of the underlying assets are known and their dependence is not. To do so, we reduce the n-asset problem to n two-asset problems of the type solved by Hobson, Laurence, and Wang (2005a), and use the Block Rearrangement Algorithm1 (BRA) to approximate the minimising dependence among the assets. The cash component of the portfolio is computed exactly, so that its price is a valid lower bound, and reassembling the BRA output with the original marginals gives an upper bound computed by quadrature; together they bracket the minimum basket-option price. In log-normal examples with three and six assets the bracket has a relative width of at most 0.1%, and the corresponding sub-replicating portfolios are sparse, using only two strikes per asset, while the resulting bounds are tighter than those obtained from a general-purpose multi-marginal optimal-transport algorithm with strikes on a grid. We also give the lower bound and an optimal portfolio in closed form in three special cases: a deep in-the-money basket, a basket with one dominant asset, and jointly mixable marginals.

entries.title: Conditional propagation of chaos for systems of particles with polynomial interactions
entries.summary: We consider N interacting particles taking values in the real numbers and evolving in discrete time with time step 1/n. Each particle follows an individual dynamics, driven by its own noise, which depends on the total configuration via a polynomial interaction. Moreover, all particles receive the same collective perturbation. This perturbation is given by a multilinear homogeneous sum of order $ m \geq 2$ of independent centered random fields which are evaluated at the current positions of the particles. We show that, as N and n tend to infinity, the system converges to the solution of a conditional McKean-Vlasov equation which is driven by an additional Brownian motion which emerges in the limit from the collective perturbations. Moreover we give explicit bounds for the Wasserstein-2-distance. Our proof combines the invariance principle of Mossel, O'Donnell and Oleszkiewicz (2010), the CLT for Wiener chaoses in the Wasserstein-2-form of Ledoux, Nourdin and Peccati (2015) and a conditional law of large numbers for weighted U-statistics proven in this paper.

entries.title: Reinforcing Few-Step Diffusion Models via Shadow Posterior Matching
entries.summary: Few-step diffusion models are widely deployed for their efficiency. However, reinforcing them with black-box rewards, as is routine for multi-step models, faces two structural challenges. First, a few-step generator is a sampler rather than a score model, so its velocity is not the forward velocity of the generated distribution. Second, it must be anchored to the undistilled teacher, which shares no transitions with it. Existing few-step RL methods handle the latter with a marginal KL to the teacher, but each pays for the former in its reward credit. We propose Shadow Posterior Matching (SPM), which renoises generated samples into shadow inputs and obtains the credit from their shadow posterior. From the KL-regularized reward objective, we derive a regression loss that turns reward values into a reward direction while anchoring the generator's outputs to the teacher and aligning the shadow inputs with the deployed inputs. Applied to 4-step generators, SPM achieves higher rewards with less reward hacking than prior few-step RL methods.

entries.title: LIFT: Latent Flow Matching for Probabilistic Cell Fate Dynamics with Single Cell Snapshots
entries.summary: Lineage tracing links cell states through clonal ancestry, but does not generally identify unique source-descendant pairings. Learning from such data therefore requires a model of conditional outcomes, rather than only the terminal population distribution. We introduce LIFT, a latent flow framework for probabilistic cell-state generation from lineage-informed couplings. Variational inference encodes alternative outcomes in a latent space, while a conditional prior enables sampling from the initial state alone. A Mean Flow decoder predicts future cell state directly, requiring one decoder evaluation per sampling, which makes it convenient to predict cell fate through large scale Monte-Carlo sampling. This construction combines a representation of one-to-many relationships with efficient sampling and an analysis of conditional prediction error. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate LIFT's ability to recover both population distribution and cell fate probabilities.

entries.title: Quantitative approximations for finite-state mean-field configuration models
entries.summary: We establish quantitative approximations for the empirical measures of finite-state mean-field particle systems in a general framework. The scales of the empirical drift and covariance distinguish the ODE and critical diffusion regimes and determine the corresponding time rescaling. In the ODE regime, we obtain quantitative central limit approximations in the $1$-Wasserstein distance and a Bernstein-type concentration inequality. The concentration bound has no dimensional prefactor. Its explicit time dependence also identifies growing intervals on which the ODE approximation remains accurate. In the critical regime, we prove a quantitative nonlinear diffusion approximation in the $1$-Wasserstein distance. We apply our quantitative approximation results to noisy voter systems, Moran models with mutations and selections, heat-bath Glauber dynamics for the $p$-spin Curie--Weiss model, and autocatalytic reactions with mutations.

entries.title: Closing Performance Gap for Diffusion Language Models under Low Inference Budgets
entries.summary: Diffusion language models offer an architectural route to low-budget generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, which can reduce the number of sequential decoding steps relative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. However, realizing this advantage at low budgets is challenging, as generation quality often declines when the number of denoising and refinement steps is reduced. Editable diffusion models address this quality loss through post-draft refinement, but useful intermediate results may still be lost before final submission. We introduce CaRR (Commitment-aware Refinement and Recovery), a training-free framework which improves submission quality from a fixed editable checkpoint through updated-context refill and trajectory-based recovery within its existing forward schedule. Token Commitment Remasking (TCR) remasks selected native pure replacements and refills them on the next scheduled edit forward using the updated context. Submission Commitment Recovery (SCR) uses the resulting refinement trajectory to recover supported candidates when the final response does not satisfy task-specific output requirements. Both modules operate within the native mask/edit schedule without additional backbone forwards. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning show consistent gains in average accuracy over native ME-DLM across four inference budgets, with the largest gains under tight budgets. At one-eighth of the full scheduled forward budget, CaRR improves the six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 pp, including gains of 11.37 and 10.05 on MBPP and MBPP+.

entries.title: Extending Rademacher Complexity-Based Generalization Theory to Domain Generalization
entries.summary: Domain generalization (DG) aims to train models on multiple source domains with distinct distributions to ensure robust performance on unseen target domains. In doing so, it elevates the concept of generalization from the traditional sample level to the distribution level. Existing theoretical frameworks introduce a domain space endowed with a meta-distribution to extend classical generalization analysis to this new setting. However, these approaches typically treat the domain space as devoid of geometry. In reality, the domain space is an inherently infinite-dimensional, nonlinear abstract space composed of probability distributions, and its complex geometric properties fundamentally determine generalization behavior. Consequently, existing geometry-free theories of domain generalization have a fundamental limitation. They lack a formal characterization of what distinguishes distribution-level generalization from sample-level generalization, leaving the inherent difficulty of generalizing across domains largely unexplained. To bridge this gap, we formalize the domain space as the Wasserstein space over the representation space. Building on the geometric properties of this space (specifically the $\mathrm{CD}(K,\infty)$ curvature theory) we derive a novel, geometry-dependent DG error bound. By introducing an additional curvature-dependent confidence term, this bound formally disentangles the two levels of generalization effects and reveals the essential nature that domain generalization is affected by both the invariance and the curvature of the representation space. Finally, we experimentally validate the effect of curvature on domain generalization.

entries.title: Physical Laws without Physics Loss? Probing Learned Dynamics in Video World Models through Forced Response
entries.summary: Do video world models learn physical laws without a physics loss, or merely imitate motion? Overall motion and appearance scores cannot settle it. We investigate this through nonlinear forced response: an excitation shakes the support of a suspended object. We introduce dual visual-numeric conditioning and adapt six image-to-video backbones to predict this motion using only the flow-matching loss. Wan predicts motion accurately and generalizes to unseen excitations, objects, poses, and scenes. Counterfactual tests suggest capabilities beyond replaying training videos. But what laws have they learned? We design three tiers of tests using Taylor expansions of the dynamics and geometry. All six reproduce the linear response, including resonance; five capture higher-order dynamics, including nonlinear softening. Remarkably, softening is barely present in training: only 0.74% of the swing's squared displacement. Extensions to a double pendulum and a rocking block show sustained dynamics are learned more faithfully than brief impacts. Yet learned dynamics may fail to appear when state estimation or propagation goes wrong. We turn these tests and findings into strategies to improve video training and generation.

entries.title: Differentially Private Score Estimation with Applications to Score-Based Generative Models
entries.summary: Estimating the score function of a distribution plays a central role in statistics and machine learning, with applications in distribution estimation, sampling, and score-based generative modeling. However, learning scores from sensitive data raises privacy concerns. These concerns are particularly pronounced in score-based generative modeling, where trained models may memorize individual training examples and expose sensitive information through membership inference and data extraction attacks. Although non-private score estimation has been extensively studied, the statistical limits of its private counterpart remain less understood. In this work, we study score estimation under $(α,β)$-differential privacy for $d$-dimensional sub-Gaussian distributions with locally $γ$-Hölder-continuous scores. We develop a sampling-based private score estimator using quadratic B-splines and the exponential mechanism, and we implement our proposal through projected Langevin Monte Carlo with runtime polynomial in the sample size $n$. The proposed estimator satisfies $(α,β)$-differential privacy, and achieves expected density-weighted squared error $\mbox{polylog}(n) \max(n^{-2γ/(d+2γ+2)},\,(nα)^{-2γ/(d+γ+1)})$. We also establish a nearly matching private minimax lower bound, thereby characterizing the privacy-accuracy trade-off for score estimation. As an application, we construct a differentially private diffusion model whose privacy guarantee is independent of the number of denoising steps. We show that, with an appropriate discretization scheme, the resulting diffusion model attains nearly minimax optimal expected total variation error among all private distribution estimators. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

entries.title: ActMem: From Latent Memory Reasoning to Grounded Robotic Action
entries.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in real-world long-horizon manipulation, where memory plays a crucial role. However, existing memory-augmented VLAs either retrieve past observations without reasoning about what they imply, or reason over the full history in a shared context where it crowds out current perception. Cognitive science treats them as distinct systems: memory reconstructs past experience to decide what to do, while perception guides how to act. We therefore propose ActMem, an in-context memory framework that decouples memory reasoning from perceptual grounding within a single vision-language backbone. Built on a vision-language model with native video understanding, ActMem infers the current subtask from a timestamped interaction history and keeps the hidden states formed during this inference as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT), which conditions a flow-matching action expert. Perception Attention further lets the expert attend directly to the current view. To keep inference fast under long histories, Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation across consecutive decisions without changing the output. ActMem achieves 71.1% task success and 80.8% completion success on RoboMemArena, surpassing the strongest baseline by 7.5 and 8.7 percentage points, and 73.8% average success on MIKASA-Robo, the best among all compared methods. In the real world, it reaches 68.8% average success on exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory tasks, 10.0 percentage points above the strongest memory-augmented VLA. Code and checkpoints will be released at https://github.com/LigphiDonk/ActMem and https://huggingface.co/donk111/ActMem.

entries.title: Quantum Calibration of Local-Volatility Surfaces from Sparse Option Quotes
entries.summary: Calibrating a volatility surface from sparse option prices requires repeated solutions of a pricing equation as the volatility parameters change. We implement a hybrid quantum and classical method for this inverse problem using the Dupire local-volatility model. A positive coefficient representation specifies the local variance, and linear combinations of Hamiltonian simulations approximate the associated pricing evolution. The circuit propagates through successive maturity intervals and evaluates discrepancies at the observed strikes. Measurement counts provide the objective values used by a classical optimiser to update the volatility coefficients. We implement this calibration cycle in a logical gate simulator and assess it alongside classical pricing solvers and alternative surface models. Multiple-maturity synthetic examples illustrate the reconstruction of smiles and skews, while a separate small circuit experiment tests the complete measured calibration. The comparisons quantify the effects of model flexibility, pricing approximation and measurement precision. Recorded gate counts and sampling budgets identify the main computational costs of the implementation.

entries.title: A joint framework for SPX, VIX and VXX
entries.summary: Options on VXX bring the dynamics of the VIX futures curve into the joint SPX-VIX calibration problem. We construct a common model by specifying the VIX and then recovering instantaneous SPX variance from the requirement that its risk-neutral conditional expected average over the next thirty days equals the squared VIX. With truncated signatures of time-extended polynomial diffusions, this recovery reduces to finite-dimensional linear algebra and gives explicit access to the futures underlying VXX. The same specification therefore governs equity variance and rolling volatility exposure. To accommodate flexible specifications while respecting variance nonnegativity, we develop a regularized model and quantify the pricing errors of its tractable VIX and VXX proxies. Applications to short-dated option smiles illustrate joint calibration across the three markets, with Monte Carlo estimates of the proxy error bounds well below quoted bid-ask spreads.

entries.title: Horizontal Flow Matching for Single-Cell Spatiotemporal Dynamics
entries.summary: Learning the spatiotemporal dynamics of cells from spatial transcriptomics requires connecting snapshots of different cells acquired in different coordinate frames. A rotation or translation of a section can appear as cell movement and distort the inferred correspondence. We introduce horizontal flow matching, which learns changes in tissue organization, molecular state, and cell abundance up to shared rigid motion. The dynamics follow a continuity--reaction equation whose action assigns no cost to shared rigid motion, and the resulting horizontal projector removes this component from spatial prediction errors during learning and from predicted velocities during generation. An equivalent endpoint problem jointly estimates correspondence and relative pose in Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao geometry and yields analytic paths whose velocity and growth serve as regression targets. Regressing these targets recovers the horizontal dynamics under ideal population conditions. Our model, HORIZON, uses an equivariant transformer to predict velocity and growth from the current tissue, so that a tissue can be generated continuously from a single initial snapshot. On a simulated tissue observed in perturbed coordinate frames, alignment improves reconstruction and projection reduces rigid drift. On four spatial transcriptomics time courses, HORIZON reconstructs tissue geometry, gene expression, and cell abundance more accurately than existing spatial and unbalanced trajectory methods, and interpolates held-out developmental stages.

entries.title: A Lions lift framework for gradient and Newtonian evolutions in Wasserstein spaces
entries.summary: To analyze evolutions driven by functionals over the space of probability measures, one can opt for the extrinsic Lions lift approach or the intrinsic Wasserstein viewpoint with its abstract metric structure. While the latter has been a successful playground for the study of first-order gradient flows, it classically relies on $λ$-convexity, and has eluded attempts of extensions to second-order Newtonian-like dynamics. Motivated by these obstructions, we show that the extrinsic Lions lift has the full capabilities to carry out the first-order gradient-flow program, which is classically done intrinsically in the Wasserstein space. As illustrated in an example, this paves the way for a framework of gradient evolutions beyond the $λ$-convex case, which is classically demanded for energies in the Wasserstein space. Furthermore, our interpretation of the Lions lift enables the formulation of a notion of second-order Newtonian curves in the Wasserstein phase space. Such curves can be constructed through a second-order JKO-like scheme and, when applied to linear and interacting energies, naturally lead to Vlasov kinetic equations and existence of solutions thereof.

entries.title: Moment approximations in optimal transport: geometric estimates and a semiclassical limit
entries.summary: We study finite moment approximations of linear optimization problems over measures. Under suitable assumptions, we establish the existence of discrete minimizers with a controlled number of support points, duality and $Γ$-convergence as the moment approximation is refined. This framework accommodates several transport problems, in which marginal constraints are replaced by finitely many moment constraints. For moment functions localized at scale $r_n$, we prove an estimate controlling $W_\infty$ by $W_p$ up to an additive error of order $r_n$, which also applies to discrete measures. For repulsive costs, we show that minimizers remain separated from the diagonal, uniformly in the number of moments, and we derive consequences for dual potentials. Finally, under a moment-correction assumption, we prove that the fermionic minimum energies converge in the semiclassical limit to the moment-constrained Coulomb transport value for a fixed family of moment functions.

entries.title: Diffusion Models are Provably Efficient Priors for Sparse Recovery
entries.summary: Diffusion models have transformed generative modeling through their ability to capture and generate samples from complex data distributions. This success has spurred substantial interest in using pretrained diffusion models as expressive priors for highly ill-posed inverse problems in imaging and sensing. Despite strong empirical performance, theoretical understanding of this approach remains limited: existing guarantees are often asymptotic or entail prohibitive computational costs in the worst case. In this paper, we address this gap by studying sparse recovery from a small number of linear measurements, a classical problem in compressed sensing. We show that, given an accurate diffusion model capturing a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior, a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler provably recovers the sparse signal in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices. When the signal is indeed drawn from the postulated prior, we further establish total variation guarantees for posterior sampling after a final denoising step. These results lay a theoretical foundation for statistically and computationally efficient inverse solvers with diffusion priors.

entries.title: Convergence of replicator-mutator particle systems via bounded Wasserstein distance
entries.summary: Interacting particle systems with selection and mutation mechanisms arise in biological modeling, evolutionary optimization, and particle filtering methods. In this work we will consider the paradigmatic replicator-mutator PDE, which combines a diffusive component with a source term that depends on an external potential. We derive quantitative error estimates for the distance between the empirical measure of an unweighted particle system and the solution of the PDE. The proof uses a Wasserstein-1 distance with a bounded ground cost, which allows us to treat unbounded potentials on an unbounded state space. The key tools are the optimal coupling of newly resampled particles and, for the time-continuous limit, the use of a discrete-time killing resampling.

entries.title: Asymptotic Error of the Euler--Maruyama Scheme for McKean--Vlasov SDEs Driven by $α$-Stable Processes
entries.summary: We study the continuous-time Euler--Maruyama error for McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equations (SDEs) driven by symmetric $α$-stable noise, $1<α<2$. We assume globally Lipschitz coefficients, a bounded jump coefficient, and bounded Lipschitz state derivatives and law-derivative kernels. The error normalized by $(n/\log n)^{1/α}$ converges jointly with the original driver in the multivariate Skorokhod $J_1$ topology, and hence stably relative to the driver's path. The limit solves a linear SDE driven by the original noise and an independent symmetric $α$-stable process. Conditional centering removes both law-derivative terms from the limiting equation. For $1\leqslant p<α$, the Euler schemes based on the numerical and exact marginal laws differ by $o((\log n/n)^{1/α})$ in the $L^p$ norm of the path supremum. Their normalized errors have the same limiting $p$th moment of the path supremum, which is positive if $σ(x_0,δ_{x_0})\partial_xσ(x_0,δ_{x_0})\ne 0$. For test functions in $C_b^2(\mathbb{R})$, the fixed-time weak error is $o((\log n/n)^{1/α})$.

entries.title: Conditional Mean-Field Type Linear Quadratic Optimal Control Problem for Regime-Switching Diffusions with Indefinite Coefficients
entries.summary: We study a conditional mean-field type linear quadratic optimal control problem for regime-switching diffusions with indefinite weights. The dynamics and cost depend on conditional expectations of the state and control given the history of the Markov chain. Under standard definiteness conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the optimal control and derive its feedback representation and optimal cost through two sets of coupled Riccati equations and a linear backward stochastic differential equation driven by the Markov chain. To treat the case of indefinite weights, we extend the equivalent cost functional approach to this setting using regime-dependent quadratic adjustments for the conditional mean of the state and its deviation from that mean. When the transformed weights in the equivalent cost functional satisfy standard definiteness conditions, this construction yields unique solvability of the original Hamiltonian system and a feedback representation of the unique optimal control. The proposed results also provide an effective method for establishing the solvability of fully coupled linear conditional mean-field forward-backward stochastic differential equations that do not satisfy certain existing monotonicity conditions. We further apply the results to conditional mean-variance portfolio selection with exogenous liability in an incomplete regime-switching market and derive the optimal investment strategy.

entries.title: Probing Physics in Motion Diffusion Models Against Their Own Estimate
entries.summary: Recent studies report that video diffusion models "know more than they show": physical properties decode better from their activations than from their inputs or outputs. But a diffusion model computes its clean-sample estimate from those same activations, so such a comparison measures how easily a readout extracts the information. Whether the model hides anything is a separate question. We set out to find hidden physical knowledge in kinematic text-to-motion diffusion models, where the physics of every intermediate estimate can be computed exactly, and recorded every layer along the sampling trajectories of MDM (two checkpoints) and MotionDiffuse. Against the usual baselines the layers do look ahead of the model's own estimate on balance and flight. With every readout tuned the same way, the estimate closes the gap: for balance and flight, adding a layer gains at most 0.01, a size that a positive control shows we would detect. The fall rate of jumps is the one clear exception. Early in denoising, MDM's layers add about 0.08 in $R^2$ (up to 0.11 in a refit) that the estimate does not yet show, and the gain fades as sampling proceeds; on MotionDiffuse it is small and not robust. The estimate also flags floating samples without training, but aborting them saves under a tenth of the compute. In a video model, plausibility that linear probes miss in Wan 2.1's clean latent becomes readable after one fixed nonlinearity.

entries.title: OpenGNS: An Open Dataset of the Gradient Noise Scale across Vision, Language, and Diffusion Models
entries.summary: The Gradient Noise Scale (GNS) metric measures the signal-to-noise ratio of gradients in stochastic gradient descent and, as shown by McCandlish et al. (2018), can be used to approximate the Critical Batch Size (CBS) during neural network training. Despite its appearance in technical reports of frontier models, no open dataset of GNS measurements across modern architectures exists, limiting systematic study of the metric. We close this gap by releasing OpenGNS, a dataset of more than 400 GNS measurement trajectories spanning three domains: image classification with ResNets, autoregressive language modeling with Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs), and image synthesis with Diffusion Transformers (DiTs), covering models from 11M to 1B parameters trained under Maximal Update Parameterization (muP) with dense batch-size and learning-rate sweeps. Building on this dataset, we study how the GNS depends on hyperparameters, scale, and training progress, and how it relates to the CBS. We find that the GNS behaves as a consistent "temperature of training", remaining stable across model sizes under muP at equivalent loss, and our results suggest task-dependent biases in its relation to the CBS: a tendency to overestimate the CBS for classification and to underestimate it for generative tasks, consistent in direction across common CBS definitions. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/olympique-marcel/OpenGNS

entries.title: Parameter estimation for discretely observed rough fractional interacting particle systems
entries.summary: We study parametric inference for interacting particle systems driven by independent fractional Brownian motions, based on discrete observations of all particles over a fixed time horizon. Our goal is to estimate an unknown drift parameter in the joint limit as the number of particles increases and the observation mesh vanishes. For $H>\frac 12$, we construct contrast based estimators by extending the discrete time least squares approach of Neuenkirch and Tindel to the interacting setting. For the rough regime $H\in(\frac 14,\frac 12)$, we introduce a modified contrast and use the stochastic sewing lemma to handle the first order approximations available from discrete observations. Our analysis combines the propagation of chaos for the associated fractional McKean Vlasov equation with estimates controlling the temporal discretization error. When the Hurst parameter and the diffusion coefficient are known, we establish strong consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed estimators. The asymptotic results reveal an interplay between the number of particles and the temporal discretization: the convergence rate with respect to the observation mesh changes at $H=\frac 34$, while the asymptotic normality holds in both regimes considered. We further develop a joint estimation procedure for the drift parameter, the Hurst parameter, and the diffusion coefficient, extending quadratic-variation methods for fractional Brownian motion to the interacting particle framework. Numerical experiments illustrate the performance of the proposed estimators.

entries.title: ViLFlow: Parallel Vision-Language Generation with Continuous Latent Flows
entries.summary: Vision-language generation has predominantly relied on autoregressive and discrete diffusion models. Autoregressive models generate tokens sequentially, while discrete diffusion models typically predict tokens independently within each denoising step. We propose ViLFlow (Vision-Language Flow), a continuous-flow vision-language model that combines joint modeling of output embeddings with parallel token decoding. ViLFlow adapts pretrained continuous language generation to visual question answering and image captioning through learned image guidance and prediction-aware token decoding. A visually adapted teacher provides image-guided predictions as additional denoising supervision. The denoiser learns to reproduce these predictions directly, retaining one image-conditioned prediction per generation step. We train the token decoder on denoiser predictions and paired reference text to improve the conversion of continuous outputs into words. The decoder can be adapted independently, improving answering and captioning without further denoiser training. For captioning, it also supplies text feedback during late denoising, allowing decoded words to inform subsequent refinement. ViLFlow outperforms autoregressive and masked-diffusion baselines by up to 8.46 percentage points on VQAv2 and 4.50 points on GQA without GQA training. On COCO Karpathy test, it improves CIDEr by 16.25 over masked diffusion and 17.81 over sampled autoregression.

entries.title: GALA: Gallery-Level Alignment for Real-Life Vision Decoding from EEG
entries.summary: Neural decoding of visual experience from electroencephalography (EEG) has achieved strong performance in intra-subject settings, but current methods fail to generalize across individuals: on the standard 200-way benchmark THINGS-EEG-2, top-1 accuracy drops from above 80% within subjects to about 32% for an unseen subject. Adapting a pre-trained encoder to new subjects and sessions typically requires labeled data, a bottleneck whose collection time severely limits practical device deployment. In a practical Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), however, the possible outcomes are known in advance and form a gallery of candidates, and the unlabeled EEG of the user accumulates as soon as the device is used. We propose a new setting, incremental transductive calibration, in which the decoder is calibrated regularly on all the unlabeled EEG received so far and on the known gallery, without any labels. This setting is closer to the conditions of a deployed BCI than the zero-shot and batch evaluations in current use. We evaluate it with a protocol in which queries arrive one at a time, with unknown and possibly unequal frequencies, and each query is decoded before it is used for calibration. In this setting, we introduce GALA : GAllery-Level Alignment, a label-free calibration method which registers the unlabeled EEG embeddings onto the gallery through shrinkage whitening, hubness correction and a Sinkhorn--Procrustes alignment with query frequencies estimated from the buffer, updated after every query. On THINGS-EEG-2, with a gallery of 200 images, it raises the top-1 accuracy on a new subject from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use. Across 60 evaluation settings that vary the gallery size, the query frequencies and the number of repetitions averaged per query, GALA is the most accurate label-free method in every setting, 6.6 points above the best competing method on average at the end of the stream.

entries.title: Central limit theorem for linear eigenvalue statistics of random spatial networks
entries.summary: The random connection model provides a flexible framework for spatial networks in which connectivity is determined by both geometry and randomness. Its vertices form a Poisson point process, and pairs are connected independently, conditional on their positions, with distance-dependent probabilities. This generalizes the hard distance threshold of random geometric graphs and accommodates long-range connections. We also consider a weighted extension in which each vertex carries a positive random weight that influences its probability of connecting to other vertices. This combination of spatial structure and heterogeneous connectivity raises the question of whether spectral fluctuations exhibit Gaussian behavior on large scales. We address this question by studying linear eigenvalue statistics $\operatorname{Tr}[f(A_n)]$ of the adjacency matrix $A_n$ of the random connection model in expanding windows $W_n$. For polynomial test functions, we establish a finite limit for the normalized variance and prove a central limit theorem under suitable connection-profile integrability and vertex mark moment assumptions. When the limiting variance is positive, the normalized statistics admit an $O(|W_n|^{-1/2})$ normal-approximation bound in both Wasserstein and Kolmogorov distance. Furthermore, under an exponential moment assumption on the vertex marks, we extend the central limit theorem to a general class of test functions $f$.

entries.title: FDM+: A Framework for Constrained Control of the 2D Radiative Transport Equation
entries.summary: Applying the frozen diffusion model (FDM) [29] to the constrained control of the 2D radiative transport equation presents several challenges. These include the dimensional difference between control variables and state functions, the resolution mismatch between traditional numerical solvers and deep learning models, and solution non-uniqueness. To address these obstacles, we propose a novel approach, FDM+, which includes three key improvements. Firstly, a decoupled prediction architecture is introduced to address the dimensional heterogeneity. Secondly, an efficient parameterization strategy resolves the resolution mismatch. Meanwhile, we derive a total error bound to analyze how the parameterization error and the model estimation error jointly affect the performance. Thirdly, the conditional distribution learned by the diffusion model is leveraged to perform design space exploration for multi-solution problems. A series of numerical experiments demonstrate that FDM+ outperforms existing methods in reconstruction accuracy and design flexibility.

entries.title: Stability analysis of stochastic differential equations with the Koopman operator
entries.summary: This paper investigates the stability of stochastic systems through the lens of the Koopman operator framework. In particular, we establish the connection between the convergence properties of the Koopman semigroup and specific stability properties of the underlying stochastic system. Moreover, we demonstrate that specific Koopman eigenfunctions capture stochastic attractivity properties and we illustrate these results with two numerical examples. This work mirrors existing Koopman operator-based stability results for deterministic systems and extends them to the stochastic framework.

entries.title: Algorithmic Market Making Can Lead to Rough Volatility Through the Order Book
entries.summary: Existing work suggests that markets can show volatility with paths rougher than those of Brownian motion. In theory this can happen when the order flow is close to instability with memory that decays as a power law. However, it is not fully clear how such order flow could arise from the predominantly algorithmic market making that characterizes order book dynamics. We show one such consistent mechanism. We treat each market maker as a desk that uses a first-order gradient rule to move the distances of its orders from the mid price toward target distances provided by an unknown oracle. We assume that distinct desks do not act synchronously in time but act whenever new information relevant to their respective oracles arrives, which each desk samples over its own characteristic lookback horizon. Across all desks the rule therefore takes the form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with information-driven (mini-batch) noise. In the continuum limit this update rule makes the volume of the order book follow a conservative stochastic partial differential equation (the Dean--Kawasaki equation) whose fluctuations drive the order flow. The distinct horizons of the desks further induce a persistent memory in the order flow that decays as a power law. Standard scaling arguments then lead to rough volatility. We confirm the key predictions of the model on simulated agents and on six months of Binance data with about 790 million orders. In liquid markets governed mainly by market makers, such as the perpetual futures of Binance, the order books are consistent with how our desks change the book.

entries.title: ReliFlow: Reliability-Calibrated Residual Transport for Combinatorial Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction
entries.summary: Predicting the transcriptional response to combined perturbations requires distinguishing interactions between interventions from errors in their individual effect estimates. The latter become more pronounced when single-perturbation evidence is sparse or withheld. We introduce a conditional flow-matching model that estimates the reliability of single-gene effects from training-only cross-fitting and uses those estimates to calibrate the additive source distribution. The velocity is decomposed into a known correction of the additive reference and a learned residual transport field. On Norman genetic perturbations, reduces mean absolute error (MAE) from 0.142 to 0.131 for unseen combinations of observed singles and from 0.198 to 0.178 when constituent singles are withheld. On held-out ComboSciPlex drug combinations, MAE decreases from 0.191 to 0.176. Non-additive residual correlation improves from 0.574 to 0.638, and component ablations identify the contribution of reliability weighting. The results indicate that accounting for uncertain constituent effects improves generalization to unseen genetic and chemical combinations, with a moderate increase in training cost.

entries.title: Berry Esseen bounds for fractional Vasicek type processes: continuous and high-frequency regimes
entries.summary: We study the estimation of the drift parameters $(a,b)$ of the fractional Vasicek process $dX_t=a(b-X_t)\,dt+dB^H_t$, driven by a fractional Brownian motion of Hurst index $H\in(0,1)$. The estimators are of moment type, built from the empirical mean and variance of the path, and are analysed in two regimes: continuous observation on $[0,T]$, and high-frequency observation at times $t_i=iΔ_n$ with $Δ_n\to0$ and $T_n=nΔ_n\to\infty$. Using the Malliavin--Stein method on the second Wiener chaos, we prove consistency of both estimators for every $H$, and quantitative central limit theorems in the Wasserstein distance: for $H<\frac34$ for the estimator of $a$, with explicit rates depending on $H$, and for every $H\in(0,1)$ for the estimator of $b$, at the rate $T^{-H}$. In the discrete regime the bounds contain an additional discretization term of order $Δ_n^{\min\{H+1/2,\,1\}}$, and for $H<\frac12$ the central limit theorem for the estimator of $b$ requires in addition $T_n^{1-2H}Δ_n^{1+2H}\to0$. A short Monte Carlo study illustrates the results.

entries.title: Infinity-Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Principal Component Analysis: Exact Reformulation, Finite-Sample Guarantee, and Efficient Algorithm
entries.summary: Principal component analysis (PCA) is a fundamental and ubiquitous technique for dimension reduction and representation learning, yet its empirical formulation remains vulnerable to distributional uncertainty. While distributionally robust optimization (DRO) offers a natural remedy, existing order-2 Wasserstein models of PCA either preserve the nominal PCA subspace or lack an exact reformulation. This paper demonstrates how the infinity-Wasserstein distance can reconcile these two desirable properties. For the resulting DRO model of PCA, we derive an exact finite-dimensional reformulation and explicitly identify a worst-case distribution attaining the inner maximum. Crucially, the reformulated objective retains samplewise residual information beyond the empirical covariance matrix, revealing a mechanism through which distributional robustness can reshape the learned principal subspace. Under the mild assumption that the true distribution has a finite fourth moment, we further establish a uniform finite-sample performance guarantee for the proposed model. An iteratively reweighted majorization-minimization algorithm is also developed to solve the resulting nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization problem, with a rigorous analysis of its convergence properties. Numerical experiments substantiate the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm and the practical effectiveness of the infinity-Wasserstein model in downstream applications.

entries.title: Error accumulation in reverse diffusion with an imperfect score: beyond path-space analyses
entries.summary: Diffusion modeling is a popular method of sampling from a complex, high-dimensional distribution $p$ using learned approximations of its (noised) score functions. Generating a single sample requires simulating the reverse diffusion process, which requires many queries to the learned scores. Thus, a priori, the learning errors can easily compound. Indeed, in existing theoretical analyses, the sampling error (as measured in total variation distance to $p$) accumulates polynomially with the horizon of the stochastic process. This is a consequence of bounding the error of the output law by the error of the law of the entire reverse diffusion path. In this paper, we demonstrate that by circumventing the "path-space" analysis, the error accumulation of the diffusion sampler can be mitigated when $p$ satisfies a Poincaré inequality. Moreover, we achieve this result as a special case of a broader framework that applies to any distribution $p$, but relaxes the error metric from total variation distance to a weaker metric capturing all sample statistics that do not "witness" the multimodality of $p$. We then zoom out from analyzing the diffusion sampler to the information-theoretic question: given a learned score with some error bound, how accurately can we identify $p$? We show that, for any given bound on the Poincaré constant of $p$, the diffusion sampler already nearly achieves optimal total variation error.

entries.title: Quadratically Regularized Medians in Metric and Wasserstein Spaces
entries.summary: In this paper, we introduce a new class of robust aggregators in Wasserstein spaces. After proving that all the commonly used Wasserstein barycenters are manipulable by one single corrupted input through a novel first-order optimality condition, we generalize both to the metric setting and to fractional exponents the concept of Lipschitz resilience introduced recently by Allouah, Guerraoui, Hoang and Villemaud. We proceed to show that adding a quadratic regularization to Wasserstein medians defined either in terms of the $W_1$-metric or linearized $W_2$-metric are resilient in that sense, by leveraging fine convexity estimates along generalized geodesics and flat interpolations. We finally show that iteratively solving the latter problem amounts to performing a Majorization-Minimization approximation of $W_2$-medians.

entries.title: Total Positivity Properties of American Options
entries.summary: Call option prices, viewed as functions of strike and time-to-expiration, are totally positive of order 2 (TP2) if the ratio of the price of a higher-strike call to a lower-strike call increases with time-to-expiration. A corresponding property applies to put option prices. Prior work has developed conditions for these properties to hold for European options; here we establish these properties for American options. The key condition we require is that log returns on the underlying asset have a log-concave density. Gaussian densities provide an important special case. Within our framework, we show that total positivity properties hold more broadly for American than European options. Empirically, we find that violations of TP2 properties are infrequent, typically small, and reverse quickly. Trades that bet against violations achieve high hit rates. Violations are more frequent among European than American options, a pattern that is qualitatively consistent with our theoretical results.

entries.title: Quantum Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport in spacetime through spatiotemporal Kirkwood-Dirac distributions and spatiotemporal states
entries.summary: Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport is a mathematical framework that determines the most efficient way to transform one probability distribution into another while minimizing a given cost function. Its central constructions include the Wasserstein distances, which quantify the space of probability distributions, and dual formulations that link to convex analysis. Its standard quantum generalization replaces probability distributions with density operators and cost function with positive semidefinite cost operator, which should be regarded as spatial quantum optimal transport. In this work, we propose the quantum optimal transport problem in spacetime through the spatiotemporal phase-space Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distribution and spatiotemporal states and through spatiotemporal state. We show that the two formalisms are equivalent and related via spatiotemporal operator frames. In the Kirkwood-Dirac phase-space formalism, the spatiotemporal distribution and the cost function are complex-valued, and the spatiotemporal couplings are Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distributions that yield the correct marginals for the local states. In the spatiotemporal state formalism, the cost operators are generally non-Hermitian, and the spatiotemporal couplings are generally non-Hermitian and yield the correct reduced local states. The Margenau-Hill phase-space distribution gives rise to a real-valued optimal transport in spatiotemporal phase space; in the spatiotemporal state formalism, this corresponds to a Hermitian spatiotemporal coupling state. We give a rigorous definitions and a careful discussion of its duality. We also introduce a spatiotemporal quantum Wasserstein metric based on a metric in spatiotemporal phase spaces and show that it satisfies the metric axioms.

entries.title: Wasserstein Target Diagram for Model Evaluation
entries.summary: The target diagram is often used in geosciences, which provides a visualization tool for model evaluation and shows the temporal or spatial matching of data. However, its construction requires paired data of equal sample sizes, limiting its application to model comparisons involving unpaired samples or probability distributions. In this study, we propose the Wasserstein target diagram based on the 2-Wasserstein distance from optimal transport. Unlike the original target diagram, the Wasserstein target diagram does not require paired data of equal sizes and evaluates models from the probability distribution perspective. We further establish that the two target diagrams coincide when the given paired data are comonotone, which is common in climate science, such as cumulative precipitation and solar radiation. Through two simulation studies and an application to wind speed distribution fitting, we demonstrate that the proposed diagram can detect the probability distribution discrepancies that the original target diagram may not distinguish. The Wasserstein target diagram therefore lifts the model evaluation to the probability level and provides a complementary approach to estimating the agreement in probability distributions.

entries.title: Correcting Flows with Marginal Matching
entries.summary: Flow matching models, ODE-based generative models, generate samples by gradually morphing a simple source distribution into a target distribution. However, these models still face challenges in optimally balancing computational efficiency with generation fidelity. While predictor-corrector schemes have been proven to help address this issue in diffusion models effectively, their application to flow matching models remains under-explored. In this work we present a novel training-based predictor-corrector framework for flow matching, which exploits the fact that the ODE can be easily reversed. Our key idea, termed Marginal Matching, is to correct samples at a particular time step in the forward ODE towards a matching marginal distribution of the backward ODE. This scheme proves to reduce a bound on the distance between the data distribution and the learned distribution, motivating two different implementations for the correction function. We show that our proposed method improves sample quality on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64, with minimal overhead in computation time.

entries.title: When Anchors Shift the Target: Advantage-Gated Adaptation for Diffusion Reinforcement Learning
entries.summary: Forward-process reinforcement learning adapts diffusion and flow-matching models by re-noising rewarded generations into regression targets. Because negative advantages induce concave updates with unbounded repulsive gradients, existing methods stabilize training using cached predictions from a moving policy copy, yet these anchors also alter what positive feedback teaches the model to fit. We formalize this conflict as anchor coupling: after separating frozen-reference regularizers, affine moving-anchor rules cannot eliminate negative curvature while preserving every positive regression target. We propose Advantage-Gated Adaptation (AGA) to decouple these roles. Positive samples retain standard target fitting, whose self-limiting update vanishes at the observed target independently of the moving anchor. Negative samples instead use the first-order tangent of the concave objective at the moving-policy prediction, preserving the local repulsion direction with a prediction-independent gradient. Within the quadratic-anchor family, these requirements uniquely determine the parameter-free gate $ω(a)=\max(-a,0)$. Because the moving copy provides local linearization rather than retention, AGA assigns long-horizon behavior preservation to a frozen pretrained reference regularized at its operating classifier-free guidance scale, interpreted through an implicit-reward lens. Across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment, our experiments show that displacing positive targets degrades visual quality and heightens sensitivity to policy-copy schedules, whereas AGA consistently improves the reward--quality trade-off.

entries.title: Generalized and Convex Poincaré Inequalities via Transport-Divergence Inequalities
entries.summary: We investigate the relationship between generalized $(q',p')$-Poincaré inequalities and transport-divergence inequalities involving $χ^q$-type divergences. Extending the classical correspondence between the $(2,2)$-Poincaré inequality and quadratic transport-$χ^2$ inequalities, we prove that a $(q',p')$-Poincaré inequality is equivalent to a transport-divergence inequality for conjugates $(p,p')$ and $(q,q')$. We then study the convex counterpart of these inequalities. Using weak barycentric optimal transport and convex order, we establish an equivalence between convex $(q',p')$-Poincaré inequalities and weak transport-divergence inequalities involving a projected $χ_q$ divergence. We further characterize the minimizers arising in this projection problem through a geometric condition on the relative density. In dimension one, we analyze the geometric consequences of $(q',p')$-Poincaré inequalities by identifying sharp conditions on the behavior of the density both at infinity and near isolated zeros. We show that when $q'>p'$, the concentration behavior becomes polynomial rather than exponential at infinity. Finally, we interpret these inequalities through the lens of optimization in Wasserstein space. In particular, the equivalence between transport-divergence and Poincaré inequalities appears as an analogue of the equivalence between quadratic growth and Polyak--Łojasiewicz inequalities in finite-dimensional optimization.

entries.title: High-Dimensional Black-Box Optimization via Guidance Sampling of Diffusion Models
entries.summary: Many real-world optimization problems involve optimizing black-box objectives for which only a limited number of evaluations are available. Bayesian optimization (BO) is a powerful framework for such problems, but its effectiveness often deteriorates in high-dimensional spaces. Recent work leverages diffusion models for black-box optimization, often through pre-training a reward-conditioned score network to steer generation towards high-reward samples. Alternatively, gradient-based guidance methods assume access to a differentiable reward function from which guidance gradients are queried. However, these approaches either require large amounts of labeled data for offline training or access to exact reward gradients, limiting their applicability in black-box settings. We propose BReaD (Black-box Reward-guided Sampling of Diffusion Model), a guidance sampling framework for optimizing black-box rewards without assuming access to a labeled dataset or reward gradients. The proposed method uses a Gaussian process (GP) as a differentiable surrogate for the unknown objective and actively queries labels for the generated samples. We provide a theoretical analysis of the total-variation distance between the generated distribution and the target distribution. Using Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) as guidance signals, our method balances exploration and exploitation during generation and enables the discovery of high-reward regions in the data space. Numerical experiments on scientific discovery and image generation tasks demonstrate that our framework can effectively optimize black-box rewards in low-data scenarios.

entries.title: Hierarchical Diffusion Transformer for End-to-End Image Generation
entries.summary: Pixel-space diffusion learns visual representations and image generation jointly in a single end-to-end training stage, without a separately pretrained visual encoder. However, plain pixel-space Transformers still trail leading two-stage latent diffusion models in generation quality and training efficiency. We hypothesize that part of this gap arises from retaining one token per patch throughout the backbone, which does not explicitly encourage a visual hierarchy that summarizes related content at progressively coarser levels. To address this, we introduce Hierarchical Diffusion Transformers (HiT), which progressively group related tokens and represent each group with a single token. The main Transformer bottleneck processes these compact group tokens, and ungrouping restores features to their original image positions. A compression budget regulates the average compression ratio across the batch, allowing group memberships and counts to vary across images and diffusion timesteps during both training and generation. The model exhibits emergent semantic structure, learning to group coherent objects and object parts without segmentation labels. In text-to-image generation, HiT further learns to group caption words with image patches depicting the same concepts, without region annotations. HiT achieves 1.48 FID on ImageNet $256\times256$ and reaches comparable generation quality to JiT using approximately 40\% of its cumulative training FLOPs. For text-to-image generation, HiT exceeds UniLiP's average score across five benchmarks with roughly $6\times$ fewer denoiser parameters and $3\times$ fewer forward FLOPs. These results suggest that learning a visual hierarchy within the generator breaks down the barrier to stronger image generation without external visual pretraining.

entries.title: Symmetries of Counterfactuals: Identification and Testability of Counterfactual Maps from Covariate Heterogeneity
entries.summary: In general, counterfactuals are not identified from data alone, because many causal models produce the same observed distributions but different counterfactuals. A common approach to circumvent this problem is to restrict the mechanism to a class in which it becomes unique, such as triangular monotone maps or optimal transport maps. However, whether the assumed class is correct is usually not examined. In this work, we study what the data can tell us when covariates are available that influence the outcome only through its latent cause. First, we characterise all counterfactual maps that are consistent with the data. They differ from the true map by a group of symmetries that preserve the conditional outcome distributions given the covariates. The more these distributions vary across covariate values, the smaller the group. Second, we show that for the classes above, consistency with the data is equivalent to a single conditional independence, which yields a test of the assumed class. We illustrate both results on synthetic data and on the ACTG 175 HIV trial.

entries.title: Path-Aligned Constraint Equivariance
entries.summary: Learned super-resolution of physical fields must satisfy structural constraints---such as divergence-free flow ($\nabla\cdot u=0$), curl-free fields ($\nabla\times u=0$), and pointwise sum-to-one normalization ($1^\top p=1$)---that standard training objectives do not enforce. Soft penalties trade fidelity against satisfaction via a scalar hyperparameter $λ$ but cannot drive the residual to zero; hard-constrained regression eliminates the residual by construction yet converges to the conditional mean, losing small-scale spectral structure. We observe that in Conditional Flow Matching with linear paths, a linear constraint $Ax=c$ is preserved along the entire transport trajectory whenever the velocity field is compatible ($Av_θ=0$) and the initial noise is consistent ($Ax_0=c$); along the trajectory, the latter two conditions are also necessary. We term this the path-equivariance principle and instantiate it in PACE (Path-Aligned Constraint Equivariance), a framework that enforces these conditions through a null-space parameterization of the velocity field and a constraint-respecting noise sampler, with no modification to the loss function or the ODE integrator. Across three constraint families, PACE reduces the mean constraint residual by one to five orders of magnitude relative to unconstrained baselines, matching the residual level of the data-generation pipeline itself. The proposed framework requires only a closed-form parameterization onto the null space of $A$; within this scope, it offers exact constraint enforcement while recovering the spectral content and predictive diversity that conditional-mean regression systematically loses, all under a single unified recipe.

entries.title: Robust Actor-Critic Learning under Transport and Divergence Uncertainty
entries.summary: Learning reliable control policies requires accounting for uncertainty in transition dynamics and errors introduced by function estimation and action generation. We develop an actor--critic method for discounted robust Markov decision processes with continuous states and actions and an unknown nominal transition law. We consider transition uncertainty sets defined by Wasserstein distance, total variation, Kullback--Leibler divergence, or Pearson chi-square divergence. A conditional diffusion model is fitted once to offline transitions. At each subsequent iteration, we estimate the robust action-value function from current-policy observations using a shared-target minimax criterion, then update a generative actor through exponentially weighted score matching. Regularization preserves exploration and provides the density regularity needed for conditional distribution estimation. Under coverage and regularity conditions, we establish finite-sample bounds for critic estimation, the learned conditional action law, and the robust return of the implemented policy. The bounds distinguish critic estimation error, uncertainty in the nominal transition model, and policy regularization, and characterize how the four robustness radii affect the resulting guarantees.

entries.title: Stochastic Diversity Windows: Diagnosing Noise Influence in Robotic Diffusion Sampling
entries.summary: Diffusion models are increasingly adopted in robotics and control due to their capability to express multiple feasible solutions to a given task. However, the role of stochasticity in the diffusion model-sampler across denoising remains poorly understood. We introduce a per-timestep counterfactual diagnostic that tests how changing the sampled noise affects the final output. Across five model-sampler configurations spanning three robotics benchmarks, diverse architectures, domains, and conditioning mechanisms, we reveal highly varied temporal sensitivity profiles, where noise-induced deviations can amplify, partially contract, or undergo near-total attenuation downstream. From these profiles, we define stochastic diversity windows (SDWs): compact intervals that identify where sampler stochasticity has the strongest measured influence on the final output. Guided by these windows, we apply two heuristic interventions: targeted stochastic amplification, which increases sample diversity exploration of the solution space, and an SDW-hybrid sampler, which replaces DDPM steps with DDIM skips in low-impact regions, resulting in network evaluation reductions of up to 40-60% and wall-clock time by up to 85%, with no consistent changes detected in feasibility, cost, or diversity across held-out tasks.

entries.title: Sub-Meter Canopy Height Synthesis from Sentinel-2 via Anchored Residual Flow
entries.summary: Canopy height models (CHMs) - per-pixel maps of vegetation top height - are essential for forest carbon accounting, wildfire fuel mapping, and tree-level ecology, yet sub-meter CHMs require airborne LiDAR refreshed on multi-year national cycles. We produce 0.5 m CHMs from free 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery, a 20$\times$ cross-modal super-resolution task where optical reflectance must predict geometric height it does not directly observe. Motivated by the perception-distortion trade-off, we derive two operating points with shared conditioning. A deterministic regressor (Anchor) targets low distortion; a conditional flow matching model, trained on the Anchor's residual in a learned CHM latent space (AR-flow), targets perceptual fidelity. Trained on 197k LiDAR-paired tiles spanning 69 ecoregions across the contiguous United States and evaluated on 2,530 held-out tiles against eight baselines, the Anchor achieves 2.83 m MAE using only free satellite input. The AR-flow reduces sliced Wasserstein distance from the Anchor's 1.13 to 0.208, at a higher MAE of 3.68 m. Crown-scale statistics improve, but strict individual-tree detection remains weak: generated sub-pixel detail represents plausible structure rather than measured individual trees. Quarterly continental refresh becomes tractable, letting satellite monitoring inform timing and extent for more expensive data acquisitions.

entries.title: Task Convergent Flow Matching for Generative Robotics
entries.summary: Successful manipulation requires the manipulated objects to progress toward a desired task outcome. Generative policies can produce plausible robot motions without ensuring this progress, allowing successive action chunks to stall or undo earlier changes to the scene. We introduce a task-centric inference-time refinement framework for flow matching policies that evaluates candidate action chunks through parallel physics-based rollouts and searches for motions satisfying sufficient conditions for task convergence. Task-level performance funnels bound temporary regressions while requiring net progress over each chunk. We establish sufficient conditions under which repeated funnel satisfaction yields convergence throughout execution, and use interval-wise Lipschitz bounds to verify continuous-time funnel satisfaction from sampled rollouts. To accommodate contact-rich hybrid dynamics, we refine the flow's source seeds using derivative-free Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), constrained to radial quantile bands of the source distribution to help retain the learned motion prior. This formulation supports both Euclidean and pose-valued Riemannian Flow Matching (RMFM) policies. On PushT and three-cube stacking, refinement raises success from 31.3% to 88.5% and from 77.0% to 86.0%. On PushT, whose coverage score responds continuously to the motion of the block, a learned funnel lowers the average maximum loss of achieved progress by 19% relative to constraining the endpoint of each chunk alone, at a similar success rate. With the radial band, 11.3% of the executed motion windows are out of distribution, a rate within the range of held-out demonstrations, compared with 34.1% for an unconstrained search.

entries.title: Beyond Strike Remapping: Conditional-Gamma Pricing of Leveraged ETF Options under Local Volatility
entries.summary: Options on leveraged ETFs (LETFs) are priced and hedged off the LETF volatility surface, but path-dependent variance drag makes that surface difficult to build consistently with the underlying index smile. We study three methods for constructing it: a closed-form first-order strike remapping, a new conditional-Gamma method, and a two-dimensional joint-law PDE that makes no distributional assumption and serves as the benchmark. The conditional-Gamma method is our main contribution. It conditions on the terminal underlying return, which preserves the state dependence of variance drag that a single remapped strike discards. Three one-dimensional forward PDEs under a calibrated local-volatility model give the conditional mean and variance of integrated variance, and a Gamma law matched to these moments keeps realised variance non-negative and prices the option in closed form. A shifted-Gamma variant that also matches the conditional third moment gives its clearest gains for inverse products at longer maturities, and a Gamma-mixture extension covers the full range of conditional skewness compatible with non-negative realised variance. On S&P 500 and Nikkei 225 surfaces the conditional-Gamma smile tracks the benchmark closely at every leverage tested, including the wings where the strike remapping drifts. A full LETF smile takes 0.85-1.42 seconds against 197-224 seconds for the benchmark, a 158- to 236-fold speed-up. Against listed TQQQ quotes the conditional-Gamma smile lies inside the market bid-ask at most strikes.

entries.title: ReMaRL: Learning to Unmask and Remask in Frozen Diffusion Language Models
entries.summary: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, and the order in which tokens are unmasked affects final-answer accuracy. Several methods learn unmasking policies from task rewards, but these policies cannot remask earlier predictions. Remasking lets the model correct those predictions using newly generated context. Heuristic rules guide both unmasking and remasking, while supervised remaskers learn to detect token errors. Neither approach directly optimizes these decisions for final-answer correctness. To address this gap, we introduce ReMaRL (Remasking with Reinforcement Learning), a lightweight policy that learns which tokens to unmask, retain, or remask. We train this roughly 0.3M-parameter policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) from final-answer rewards while keeping the diffusion model frozen. With LLaDA-8B-Instruct, ReMaRL achieves the highest scores among the compared unmasking and remasking policies within the tested inference budgets of 4-32 model calls on math and 8-16 calls on code.
